items.title: Effect size matters as much as significance
items.claim: A study reports a 'highly significant' effect (p < 0.001) of a school intervention. What further information do you need?

options.text: The effect size (e.g. Cohen's d, standardised mean difference). A trivial effect can be highly significant with a large sample; a substantial effect can be non-significant with a small sample. Significance and magnitude are different questions
Only the title of the paper

items.reveal:
Cohen's d conventions (1988): 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. Education research (EEF, Hattie's meta-analyses) often reports effect sizes in months of additional learning progress.

The ASA Statement on p-values (2016) explicitly warned against treating p < 0.05 as sufficient. Recommendations: report effect sizes with confidence intervals; treat 'significance' as one piece of evidence, not as a binary verdict.
items.why: Newspaper science writing usually reports significance, not magnitude. The interesting question for policy or practice is almost always how big the effect is.

items.title: Deinstitutionalisation reduced asylum populations dramatically
items.claim: Following Italy's Basaglia Law (1978), the UK's Care in the Community policy (1980s-90s) and similar reforms elsewhere, what happened to inpatient psychiatric populations?

options.text: Inpatient populations fell by 60-90% in most Western countries by 2000. Outcomes were mixed: better integration for many, but inadequate community resources left some patients homeless or in the criminal justice system
Inpatient care was completely eliminated everywhere

items.reveal:
UK psychiatric inpatient beds: ~150,000 in 1955, ~22,000 by 2010. The shift was driven by both ideology (asylum critique, e.g. Goffman 'Asylums' 1961) and pharmacology (chlorpromazine, 1952).

Where community resources followed (Trieste, Italy under Basaglia), outcomes were generally positive. Where they didn't (UK and US in different ways), gaps in care emerged — over-representation of severely mentally ill people in prisons and homelessness is widely documented.
items.why: Major mental health policy changes have decades-long consequences. The reduction in coercive asylum care was widely accepted; the under-investment in community alternatives is the unresolved part.

items.title: The serotonin hypothesis
items.claim: A 2022 umbrella review by Moncrieff et al. examined the link between serotonin and depression. What did it conclude?

options.text: Strong evidence supports the simple chemical-imbalance model
It found no consistent evidence that depression is caused by low serotonin
It confirmed dopamine is the primary cause
It showed antidepressants do not work at all

items.reveal_title: The simple chemical-imbalance story is not well supported
items.reveal:
Moncrieff et al. (2022, Molecular Psychiatry) found no convincing evidence that depression is caused by reduced serotonin activity.

The review did not address whether antidepressants help, only whether the serotonin-deficit model holds.
items.why: Effective treatments do not require correct causal stories. Aspirin was used long before its mechanism was understood.
